podcast.title: David Usher's Solo Career
podcast.body: During Moist's 12-year break, singer David Usher embarked on a successful solo career, releasing seven albums independently. This allowed him to maintain a strong musical presence outside of the band. "Singer David Usher went solo releasing seven albums on his own."

podcast.title: Early 1990s Prime Time Success
podcast.body: Moist was among the Canadian bands that gained "a shot at prime time" in the early 1990s, indicative of the growing Canadian music scene. "The early 90s were pretty amazing with a long list of Canadian bands getting a shot at prime time. We had moist, the watchman, lowest of the low, sons of freedom, grapes of wrath, rhymes with orange, pure Gandarva's limb lifter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation and Genre
podcast.body: Moist formed in Vancouver and gained widespread popularity by aligning with the "Grunge Wave" of the 1990s, producing mid-tempo songs that were highly successful on radio. Their sound became a staple of the Canadian rock scene. "They were formed in Vancouver and rode the Grunge Wave with a series of mid-tempo songs that worked very well on the radio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Kevin Young's Freelance Writing
podcast.body: Keyboardist Kevin Young utilized the band's hiatus to work as a freelance writer. This highlights his diverse creative pursuits outside of his musical career. "keyboardist Kevin Young worked as a freelance writer."

podcast.title: Mark McAway's Book
podcast.body: Guitarist Mark McAway authored and published "The Indy Band Bible," a book offering crucial advice to emerging bands. This demonstrates his contribution to the music community beyond his performance career. "Guitarist Mark McAway published a really good book called The Indy Band Bible which offers some very important advice to anyone starting a group."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Paul Wilcox's Injury and Band Hiatus
podcast.body: During a tour supporting the *Mercedes 5 and Dime* album, drummer Paul Wilcox suffered a back injury that prevented him from performing live. This incident prompted the band to take a 12-year hiatus after the tour concluded. "It was during a tour for that last album that drummer Paul Wilcox heard his back and had to bow out of live performances and once the group limped to the end of that road trip they decided to take a break and that break lasted 12 years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reunion and Lineup Changes
podcast.body: Moist officially announced their reunion in June 2013, accompanied by "a couple of lineup changes." The band has since remained active, continuing to record and perform live. "The announcement came in June 2013 with a couple of lineup changes and the band continues to record and perform today."

xref.title: Chowder's Post-Band Career
xref.body: Bass player "Chowder" later worked with Moist and David Usher. He now works at a BMW motorcycle shop and occasionally performs at quiet, anonymous gigs and open mics, indicating a partial return to music. "Chowder, the bass player, later worked with Moist and David Usher, now works at BMW in the motorcycle shop and still plays the odd time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Christian Samson's Post-Band Career
xref.body: Drummer Christian Samson played with Edwin after his departure from I Mother Earth, had brief stints with Moist and the prog rock group Saga, and now manages his own HVAC condo service. This shows a diverse career path both within and outside the music industry. "drummer Christian Samson played around with Edwin after he left I Mother Earth. There was also a short stint in Moist and with saga, the Prague Rock Group, and he's now running his own HVAC condo service."

xref.title: Vocal Style Development
xref.body: Ben, the vocalist, initially spent the first five years of the band trying to emulate other singers like Eddie Vedder, Scott Weiland, and Zack de la Rocha. He eventually realized he couldn't sound like them and developed his own distinctive style. This unique vocal approach, combined with Ian's guitar playing, helped the band stand out from other Canadian bands of the era like Moist, Treble Charger, and The Tea Party. "I, the first five years of being in a band, you know, I was trying to sound like other people, you know, I was trying to sound like Eddie Vetter. I was trying to sound like Scott Watt. I'm trying to sound like Zack Delroch. You know, like, I'm trying to do that. And then I realized I can't do that, you know, so I just kind of ended up being me."
